lesson.title: Every Circuit Has a Simple Twin: Norton's Theorem
lesson.summary: Norton's Theorem shows that any linear network, viewed from two terminals, behaves exactly like one current source in parallel with one resistor, found from the short circuit current and the zeroed-source resistance.
lesson.body:
Real circuits are often messy: multiple sources, multiple resistors, all feeding into whatever load you actually care about. Norton's Theorem makes a remarkable promise about all of that mess: no matter how complicated the source network is, as long as it is linear, everything connected to a given pair of terminals can be replaced, from the load's point of view, by just one current source in parallel with just one resistor. The load cannot tell the difference between the real network and this simplified stand in, because they produce identical voltage and current at the terminals for any load you attach.

Finding the two numbers is a two step process. The Norton resistance, RN, is found by turning off every independent source in the network, replacing voltage sources with short circuits and current sources with open circuits, and then computing the resistance looking back into the terminals. The Norton current, IN, is the current that would flow if you shorted the terminals together directly, the short circuit current. These two numbers are not independent facts to memorize separately, they are related to the open circuit voltage, VTh, that you would measure at the terminals with nothing attached, by VTh equals IN times RN, which is just Ohm's law applied to the equivalent circuit itself.

Here is a worked example. An 18 volt source drives a 6 ohm resistor, R1, in series to a node, and from that node a 12 ohm resistor, R2, runs to ground. The terminals of interest are across R2. To find RN, turn off the 18 volt source, replacing it with a short, which puts R1 and R2 in parallel as seen from the terminals: RN equals (6 times 12) divided by (6 plus 12), which is 72 divided by 18, or 4 ohms. To find IN, short the terminals directly: this shorts out R2 entirely, so the only path for current is the source through R1, giving IN equals 18 divided by 6, or 3 amps.

As a check, VTh should equal IN times RN, which is 3 times 4, or 12 volts. Verifying independently using the ordinary voltage divider on the original circuit, with the terminals open, VTh equals 18 times R2 over (R1 plus R2), which is 18 times 12 over 18, or 12 volts exactly. The two methods agree, confirming RN equals 4 ohms and IN equals 3 amps are correct.

Norton's Theorem is built entirely from tools already in hand: Ohm's law to compute the zeroed source resistance, and Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws to compute the short circuit current in more complicated networks where a simple series or parallel reduction is not available. Its real value shows up when a circuit will be tested with several different loads, since once RN and IN are found, evaluating a new load takes seconds instead of a full re-analysis.

It is also worth being explicit about what gets zeroed and why. A voltage source with 0 volts across it is indistinguishable from a plain wire, which is exactly what a short circuit is, so replacing a voltage source with a short is simply setting its value to zero while keeping the branch intact. A current source with 0 amps flowing through it is indistinguishable from an open gap, since no current means no connection is doing any work, so replacing a current source with an open circuit is the same idea applied to the other source type. Both operations only apply to independent sources, never to a dependent source whose value depends on some other current or voltage elsewhere in the circuit, since a dependent source is not something you can simply turn off without changing the circuit's behavior.
